About the Platform

Canada's approach to critical minerals reflects the importance of secure and resilient supply chains, responsible resource development and constructive international cooperation. This platform brings together key information on Canada's 34 critical minerals and its engagement with partners abroad, providing a common basis for policy discussion and further research.

A Practical Policy Resource

The platform offers a concise view of the mineral, economic and international dimensions of Canada's critical minerals landscape. It is intended to support informed exchanges among researchers, public officials, students and other interested users.

Minerals, Production and Trade

The mineral profiles introduce the list issued by the Government of Canada and explain the principal uses and strategic relevance of each mineral. The production and international trade sections complement these profiles with 2025 data on Canadian output, export values and principal markets.

International Engagement

The consolidated MOU and partnerships register focuses exclusively on international arrangements related to critical minerals, while preserving the distinction between the two types of instruments. The policy map provides a country view of this engagement and allows users to consult the arrangements associated with each partner.

Scope and Interpretation

The data and policy instruments are presented with their original sources and relevant qualifications. Production and trade classifications do not always correspond to individual minerals, while cooperation instruments differ in legal form and scope. These distinctions should be considered when comparing records.

Project Background

Critical minerals have moved from a specialized resource-policy issue to a central question in economic and foreign policy. They support clean energy, transportation, digital infrastructure and defence, yet their supply chains are concentrated and difficult to replace quickly. Canada approaches this landscape as a mineral producer, an advanced economy and a close trading partner of the United States, Europe and the Indo-Pacific. The project examines how these roles can be brought together through practical policy, credible partnerships and a clearer understanding of Canada's strengths and dependencies.

Criticality depends on context

A mineral is considered critical when its economic or strategic importance is combined with a meaningful risk of supply disruption. The balance varies by country. Governments may examine import concentration, expected demand, the availability of substitutes and the time required to develop new production or processing capacity. They also consider whether a mineral is needed for defence, energy systems, advanced manufacturing or essential infrastructure. Critical-minerals lists are therefore policy tools rather than permanent scientific classifications. Canada's list provides a common national reference, but the relative importance of individual minerals can change with technology, markets and geopolitical conditions. The platform's mineral profiles help users move from the general list to the distinct properties, applications and policy relevance of each mineral.

Canada's role as a producer

Canada has significant geological resources, established mining expertise and experience in responsible resource governance. Those advantages create opportunities, but production figures alone do not describe Canada's position in a supply chain. Minerals may be mined in one country, processed in another and incorporated into components elsewhere before reaching a final market. Commercial viability depends on dependable buyers, infrastructure, processing capacity, investment and long-term demand. Canada must therefore consider how domestic production connects with allied economies and global value chains. The production section of this platform shows available 2025 output in the units reported by Statistics Canada, while the broader project asks how Canadian capacity can contribute to secure, competitive and responsibly managed supply relationships.

Canada as a producer

Trade and economic statecraft

Critical-minerals policy extends beyond mine development. Trade rules, investment screening, export finance, transportation corridors, ports and public support for processing can all influence where supply chains develop. Defensive measures may be used to protect sensitive assets or respond to economic coercion. Positive measures can help Canadian projects reach markets, attract capital and become reliable parts of international production networks. The challenge is to use these instruments in a coordinated and predictable way. The platform's international trade data provides a practical view of Canadian export values and leading destinations in 2025. The project places those commercial flows within a wider policy discussion about resilience, diversification and the infrastructure required to connect Canadian resources with partners abroad.

Project perspective

Trade, investment and economic statecraft

Wolfgang Alschner | 0:47

How trade and investment measures, infrastructure, ports and export financing can support Canada's position in international supply chains.

International partnerships

No country can efficiently build every stage of every critical-minerals supply chain on its own. Cooperation can provide access to resources, technology, processing capacity, investment and stable markets. Canada works with close allies that share economic and security interests, while also engaging mineral-producing and emerging economies whose participation is essential to diversified supply. These relationships take different forms. Some are formal memoranda of understanding, while others are partnerships, declarations, action plans or broader cooperation frameworks. They also differ in legal force, scope and stage of implementation. The consolidated register and policy map document these distinctions, identify the countries and institutions involved, and connect each record to an open source so users can assess the substance of the arrangement directly.

Project perspective

International partnerships

Wolfgang Alschner | 0:57

Together, these perspectives explain why the project combines mineral-level information, production and trade data, and international policy instruments. The platform is intended to support informed discussion rather than prescribe a single strategy. Its methodology, limitations and sources are documented separately so that users can interpret the evidence with appropriate care.

Foreign Ownership in Canadian Critical-Mineral Projects

This section maps Canadian critical-mineral sites — exploration projects, producing mines and processing facilities — and shows which of them have foreign owners, partners or government backing. Select any marker on the map to see that site's operator, its foreign partners and owners, and the ownership structure behind them.

Of the 138 sites mapped, 93 have some foreign involvement. The character of that involvement changes along the value chain: at the exploration stage foreign money more often arrives as a partner alongside a Canadian operator, while producing mines and processing plants are more often foreign-owned outright. Coverage is Canada's 34 critical minerals; gold, coal, cement, limestone and scrap-metal operations are excluded. Data as of 2026-09-09.

Complete Site Register

One row per site. The foreign-countries column lists every foreign owner, parent or partner identified for that site. An empty entry means foreign participation was looked for and none was found, not that the site was not checked.

Disclaimer

These are counts of sites, not production. A smelter complex and a small graphite mine each count as one. Nothing here measures output, capacity, employment or dollar value. A country with many sites is not necessarily a large presence.

Most country totals are really one company. Brazil's presence is almost entirely Vale's facilities around Sudbury. Switzerland's is Glencore. United Kingdom/Australia is Rio Tinto, one dual-domiciled firm rather than two stakes, and splitting it double-counts. Read these as company footprints, not national strategies.

Being listed says nothing about the size of a stake. A site with a 5% foreign partner looks the same here as one that is wholly foreign-owned. The percentages are in each site's ownership summary. Check them before treating a listing as significant.

The foreign-state flag covers very different things. It spans the US Department of Defense granting money to a Yukon project, Orano, which is 90% French state-owned, holding 42% of a Saskatchewan uranium mine, and Taiwan holding about 20% of a steelmaker that holds 15% of a Quebec iron ore company. The flag on its own means little; the note attached to each site is the substance.

Ownership changes constantly. Mines are bought and sold, partners come and go. Every record carries a source link and a date, and some are already out of date. The underlying site data lags too. Natural Resources Canada still lists Glencore at Kidd Creek, sold to Discovery Silver in June 2026, and Compass Minerals at Wynyard, sold in March 2026. Corrections we found are noted in the ownership summaries. Others will remain.

Two coding oddities are worth flagging. South Uchi is coded as a lithium project by NRCan but operated as a gold project, and appears here because NRCan's commodity coding places it among critical minerals. Niobec appears twice, as the mine and its ferroniobium converter about 100 m apart, because NRCan records them separately. They are one operation.

Site locations, operators and commodities come from Natural Resources Canada (Map 900A "Principal Mineral Areas, Producing Mines and Oil and Gas Fields" and "Top 100 Exploration Projects"). Ownership is original research. NRCan publishes an operator for each site but no ownership structure, and none at all for exploration projects, so every site here had its ownership researched individually from company disclosure, regulatory filings and trade press. The records vary in strength. Follow the source link on any site the argument depends on.

Partnerships and Cooperation Frameworks

Strategic partnerships, declarations, action plans and other cooperation instruments.

The G7 Critical Minerals Production Alliance

The Critical Minerals Production Alliance is a Canada-led G7 initiative to diversify production and processing of critical minerals outside China. It was launched alongside the G7 Critical Minerals Action Plan at Kananaskis in June 2025. Three rounds of announcements have followed: Toronto in October 2025, the PDAC convention in March 2026, and the Evian summit in June 2026. The cumulative total reported by the Prime Minister's Office is 69 partnerships and $19.2 billion.

The $19.2 billion figure measures the capital cost of the projects the Alliance reports having catalysed. It is not a total of funds committed by governments or partners. The dollar figures disclosed across the three backgrounders sum to $4.1 billion. Excluding offtake contracts, guarantees and letters of interest, which do not transfer capital to a project, $1.6 billion remains. The largest single figure, Greenland Resources' US$2 billion, is the value of a ten-year molybdenum supply contract with the Finnish steelmaker Outokumpu rather than an investment in the project.

$19.2B Project capital the Alliance says it has catalysed
$4.1B Actually disclosed across all instruments
$1.6B Of that, capital flowing to projects
23 of 47 Announced items that are actual projects

Announced amounts, not disbursed. Many entries are memoranda of understanding, letters of intent or conditionally approved investments. Of the 65 individual instruments announced, 32 carry no disclosed amount at all. Canadian and US dollar figures are added without conversion.

Reconciling the round totals: round one reported $6.4 billion and round two $12.1 billion, and the March 2026 release put the cumulative at $18.5 billion. Round three reported a further "more than $5 billion", while the cumulative figure given at Evian was $19.2 billion. Neither backgrounder explains the difference. One explanation consistent with the underlying data is that projects announced in more than one round are counted once in the cumulative total: seven participants appear in multiple rounds, in most cases with a further instrument attached to the same asset. The round figures should therefore not be added together.

Composition of the announcements

Just under half of the announced items are projects. The remainder are country-level agreements, research and development grants, and capacity-building grants to universities and international organisations. The headline capital figures attach to the strategic projects rather than to the full list.

Counts are of announced items. The government's own tally of 69 counts each instrument separately, so one project with a memorandum, an offtake and a letter of interest can appear three times. Each item here is one project or initiative with its instruments collapsed.

Partner countries

Germany and the United States each appear in seven announced items, Italy in five, and Japan, France and the United Kingdom in four each. Twenty partner countries appear in total, including several outside the G7: Estonia, Portugal, Greenland, Denmark, Finland and Sweden, in most cases through an export credit agency or a single industrial partner. Canada is the convenor and principal funder and is excluded from the chart below on that basis.

Where the projects are

Projects are concentrated in Quebec and Ontario, where most of the graphite, rare earth and phosphate assets are located and where the announced processing facilities are planned. Two entries are outside Canada: the Malmbjerg molybdenum project in Greenland, and NORAM's lithium technology agreement, which supplies a refinery in Portugal.

Markers are placed on the town or region named in the announcement, not on survey coordinates. Where a project also appears in this platform's mining dataset, that dataset's site coordinates are used. One item, a memorandum covering projects across New Brunswick, British Columbia and Yukon, has no single location and is not mapped.

Every announced project and initiative

All 47 announced items across the three rounds, compiled from the three official backgrounders.

The instruments behind the figures

One row per announced financial instrument, allowing the headline figures to be reconciled. The capital column records whether the amount represents capital flowing to the project; offtake contract values and export credit guarantees do not.

Scope and limitations

The Alliance records what allied governments have announced, which differs from what has been financed or built. It is therefore not a complete account of foreign involvement in Canadian critical minerals. Four of these projects correspond to sites mapped in the Projects tab; most of the remainder are processing facilities, research projects or early-stage developments outside the scope of that dataset. Figures and status are as announced on the dates shown.

Methodology and Limitations

This section explains how the platform's evidence should be interpreted. It identifies the principal limits of the production, trade and policy data, as well as the computational choices used to present them. The platform is designed as a policy reference and should be read alongside the original sources.

1 Scope and coverage

  • The platform covers Canada's list of 34 critical minerals, available 2025 production and trade information, and international arrangements with an explicit critical minerals connection.
  • Coverage reflects the public sources available when the platform was compiled. It is not an exhaustive inventory of confidential, subnational or commercially negotiated activity.
  • The dates, definitions and reporting practices of the underlying sources are not always identical.

2 Production data

  • Statistics Canada does not publish directly comparable 2025 production figures for every critical mineral. A missing figure should not be interpreted as evidence that Canada produced none of that mineral.
  • The platform retains the units and product descriptions used in the original tables. Some observations refer to mineral products or compounds rather than contained mineral quantities.
  • Records drawn from different tables should not be added together unless their units, products and statistical concepts are compatible.

3 International trade data

  • The trade section presents customs-based export values. These values are distinct from mine output, processing capacity and domestic availability.
  • Customs classifications may combine several minerals, compounds or stages of processing. A trade category may therefore be broader than an individual mineral profile.
  • The recorded destination is not necessarily the final place of consumption, and export value alone does not measure supply chain dependence or resilience.

4 MOUs and partnerships

  • The register reconciles several public sources and consolidates duplicate references to the same arrangement.
  • Partnership is a presentation category covering instruments with different legal forms, durations, financing arrangements and implementation mechanisms.
  • Public sources may not identify every amendment, implementation measure or termination. Current status is therefore limited to what can be supported by the cited material.
  • Multilateral arrangements are linked to each participating country on the map but remain a single record in the register. European Union records are also presented separately from individual countries.

5 Policy map and country shading

  • Countries are shaded according to the total number of MOUs and partnerships linked to them. Darker shading represents a larger number of documented arrangements.
  • The counts are descriptive. They do not assess legal force, funding, implementation quality, economic value, diplomatic importance or policy effectiveness.
  • Country and regional groupings are used for visualization and do not imply a position on status, sovereignty or boundaries.

6 Computational limits

  • The platform is a static HTML application. It does not connect to a live database and does not update automatically.
  • Tables, charts and indicators reflect the files embedded when the platform was generated. Changes in an external source will not appear until the platform is rebuilt.
  • Interactive performance can vary by browser and computer because the data, images and visualizations are packaged locally.
  • The platform applies filtering, grouping, deduplication, rounding and display transformations. It does not perform forecasting, causal analysis or predictive modelling.
